Of course. Here is some parent-facing guidance written in plain, accessible language. It is designed to be reassuring, clear, and to directly address the common concerns parents have.

***

### **Helping Every Child Succeed in Maths: Our New Approach**

Dear Parents and Carers,

We’re writing to you today to share some exciting news about how we will be teaching mathematics at our school. We know that for many of us, our own experiences with maths at school were not always positive. We want to make sure every single one of our students feels confident and capable in maths.

Starting next term, we will be moving to **mixed-attainment groups** for all our maths classes.

We understand this is a big change, and you will likely have questions. This guide is here to explain what we are doing and, most importantly, *why* we are doing it.

#### **What is changing?**

*   **The Old Way (Streaming):** In the past, we put students into different maths classes based on how well they’ve done in past tests. You might have known these as "sets" or "streams."
*   **The New Way (Mixed-Attainment):** Now, all students will learn together in the same classroom, with a mix of different experiences and confidence levels.

#### **Why are we making this change?**

This decision is based on a lot of research and on what we’ve seen works best to help children succeed in the long run. Here are the main reasons:

**1. There is no such thing as a "maths brain."**
For a long time, people thought you were either born a "maths person" or you weren't. We now know this is not true. Everyone can be good at maths with the right teaching and a positive attitude. Putting children into groups can give them the wrong idea—that they are either "good" or "bad" at maths for life. This simply isn’t true, and we want to break that cycle.

**2. It raises confidence and ambition for everyone.**
When we put children in a "lower" group, we can accidentally send them the message that we don’t expect as much from them. Their confidence can drop, and they can stop trying. In a mixed group, everyone is challenged and expected to do well. We find that students’ confidence and their love for learning grows.

**3. It leads to deeper, better learning for all students.**
This is the part that can seem confusing, so let’s break it down:

*   **For students who find maths tricky:** They will be in a classroom where they can hear different ways of solving a problem from their classmates. They will get support from the teacher and their peers, and they won’t feel left out or labelled.
*   **For students who usually find maths easy:** They will not be held back. In fact, they will get a much deeper understanding. The best way to check if you *really* understand something is to try and explain it to someone else. These students will become leaders in the classroom, strengthening their own skills by talking about their ideas and showing others how they got their answer. The work will challenge them to think harder, not just do more of the same.

#### **Answering Your Questions**

We know you may have worries. Here are answers to the most common ones.

**"But won't my child, who finds maths easy, get bored and be held back?"**
No. The teacher will plan lessons that have something for everyone. Think of it like building with LEGOs. Everyone might start with the same pile of bricks (the same problem), but some will build a simple house, while others will be challenged to build a huge, detailed castle. The work will be more challenging and interesting, not just more worksheets. Your child will be pushed to think more deeply.

**"My child already struggles with maths. Won't they be left behind and feel stupid?"**
The opposite is true. They will have more support than ever. Instead of being in a room where everyone is stuck, they will be in a classroom full of different ideas. The teacher will be there to support them, and they will also learn from their friends. Seeing that everyone finds some things hard helps build confidence.

**"How can one teacher possibly teach a whole class of different abilities?"**
Our teachers are trained in this! They will use a variety of methods:
*   **Group work:** Students work together, sharing ideas and helping each other.
*   **Targeted questions:** The teacher will ask different questions to different students to make sure everyone is thinking hard.
*   **Rich tasks:** The problems will be designed so that there are many ways to solve them. A student who is less confident can find a starting point, while a more confident student can find a more complex solution.

#### **How You Can Help at Home**

Your support is the most important thing of all. You don’t need to be a maths expert to help!

*   **Be positive about maths.** Avoid saying things like "I was bad at maths." Instead, say, "Maths can be tricky, but we can figure it out together."
*   **Praise effort, not just the right answer.** Say "I love how you kept trying on that hard problem!" This teaches them that hard work is what matters.
*   **Talk about everyday maths.** Point out maths when you’re shopping, cooking, or telling the time. This shows them that maths is a useful, real-world skill.

We are truly excited about this change and believe it will help all our students become more confident and capable mathematicians. Your child’s success and happiness is our number one priority.

If you have more questions, please do not hesitate to contact [Name of Head of Maths or Headteacher] to arrange a chat.

Sincerely,

[Your School Name]
